tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

schema.name: Workflow
schema.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

1	# Issue #230: a web control surface on the remote port (investigation notes)
2	
3	I read CLAUDE.md, docs/lessons.md, docs/remote-client.md §§0, 4.1–4.7 and 5–6, and the remote section of docs/design.md (3107–3584). Line numbers below are as they stand in this worktree (branch `dispatch/230-…`, clean, at 7fe8949). There is no `web/` directory yet.
4	
5	## The on-disk record and how it is rehydrated
6	
7	Persistent state on the host is the same as today. The browser adds no new kind of record.
8	
9	- **`<data dir>/devices.json`**, a `Vec<PairedDevice>` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96-106`): `id`, `name`, `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`. A browser is one more entry. The name is capped at 64 chars in `AppCore::new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs:159-170`), and the scope comes from the open window. It is written through `Effect::SaveDevices` (`src/app.rs:2910`). `last_seen` is saved at most every 300 s (`src/core/remote.rs:18`, `DeviceSeen` at 72-85). Nothing in the record says what kind of client a device is, so a "browser" field would be a schema change. The name string alone needs none.
10	- **`<data dir>/identity.json`** (`Identity`, `src/ports/remote.rs:26-41`, `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1` at :17): the server id, the name, the base64 DER certificate, `spki_sha256` and `listen {lan, port}`. The key sits in the Keychain under `remote-key:<server_id>`.
11	  - `make_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`) builds the certificate with `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`. So it has **no subjectAltName**, only a CN `Switchboard <id>`. Its validity is rcgen's default, which the doc comment gives as running to year 4096. It sets no EKU.
12	  - If the plan wants a certificate browsers accept more readily (SAN for the IP or a `.local` name, a shorter validity, serverAuth EKU, a download path), the certificate would have to be **reissued over the same key**. The SPKI and every native pin stay valid (§5 says so), but `identity.json`'s `certificate` changes. The file layout does not change.
13	  - A SAN tied to an IP would go stale when the address moves.
14	- **The pairing window** is core state only (`PairingWindow`: `until`, `code`, `scope`, `failures`; `src/core/remote.rs:45-52`) and is never saved. The QR payload is built in the UI from it every frame (`src/ui/remote.rs:154-172`).
15	- **The page itself** is compiled into the binary (`include_str!`), so there is nothing to rehydrate on the host. A page left open on a phone after the host updates itself keeps the old JS until it is reloaded. `/info` already carries `version` (`src/app.rs:3568-3604`).
16	
17	Rehydration on the device lives in the browser, not in Switchboard:
18	
19	- **The token** lives in a cookie jar or in `localStorage`, depending on decision 2.
20	- **The certificate exception** lives in the browser's store.
21	- **The flow on reload:**
22	  1. `GET /` with no auth.
23	  2. `GET /api/v1/info`.
24	  3. One authenticated read: 200 shows the sessions, 401 shows "pair again / revoked".
25	  4. Open `/api/v1/events`, then snapshot and reconcile per §4.4. A new `epoch` means refetch everything.
26	
27	What the tree implies for rehydration:
28	
29	- Host restart: same certificate, same tokens. The page reconnects and sees a new epoch.
30	- Key rotation (`src/app.rs:2776-2852` clears `devices.json`): the browser meets a **different certificate** at the same address. Its stored exception presumably no longer applies, so it shows its own interstitial before any page script runs. The page's "identity changed, pair again" state would then not be what the owner sees on a rotation. Whether that holds depends on how the browser scopes the exception (see Open questions).
31	- Address change (DHCP): a new origin. Cookies and `localStorage` are keyed by host, so the token is not found and the device pairs again, leaving the old record in `devices.json` until revoked.
32	
33	## What exists, file by file
34	
35	### `src/adapters/remote.rs` (listener, HTTP, WebSocket)
36	
37	- `RemoteRequest` (:359-371) keeps only `method`, `path`, `query` (undecoded), `body`, `bearer` and `upgrade` (the `Sec-WebSocket-Key`).
38	  - `read_request` (:444-516) parses every header into a local `Vec` and then drops all but `content-length`, `authorization: Bearer`, `upgrade` and `sec-websocket-key`.
39	  - **No `Cookie`, `User-Agent`, `Origin`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, `Accept` or `If-None-Match` reaches the frame.** Decisions 2 and 6 and any Origin check need new fields here.
40	- `RemoteReply` (:389-393) is `{status, body, authenticated}`. **It carries no headers.**
41	  - `respond` (:530-553) writes `Content-Type: application/json` on every reply, plus `Content-Length` and `Connection: keep-alive`, and nothing else. It also has a fixed reason table.
42	  - Serving HTML/CSS/JS with their types, a CSP, `Cache-Control`, `Set-Cookie`, `X-Content-Type-Options` or a 304 needs `RemoteReply` (or a separate static path) to carry a content type and headers.
43	  - `respond_upgrade` (:519-527) writes a bare 101 with no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`.
44	  - These are adapter types, not `ports/` contract types, so changing them is not bound by the additive-only rule. Tests construct the request literal at :1045-1061.
45	- Pools and accept:
46	  - `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `MAX_PAIRED = 12` (:567-568).
47	  - The accept loop (:687-718) closes a 5th unauthenticated TCP connection **at accept, by dropping it**.
48	  - A connection moves to the paired pool only when a reply comes back with `authenticated: true` (:829-844).
49	  - So a browser fetching `/`, a CSS file, a JS file and `/api/v1/info` over parallel keep-alive connections stays wholly in the unauthenticated pool. That holds while the static replies are `authenticated: false`, and even with a cookie unless static replies authenticate.
50	  - Idle connections are held up to `IDLE_TIMEOUT = 30 s` (:573).
51	  - One browser can therefore fill the four slots and have its next connection dropped. That includes the one that would carry `/pair`.
52	- Rate windows: `Limits::limited` (:631-640) counts only `PAIR_PATH` (6/min) and `INFO_PATH` (60/min) (:583-587). A static path counts against nothing today. Note that **a page load that calls `/info` spends one of the 60**.
53	- Deadlines: 5 s for the handshake and the first request line (:570). A browser that opens a connection speculatively and sends nothing for 5 s is closed. That is harmless, but it holds a slot meanwhile.
54	- `connection` (:770-876) hands every request to the frame over the bounded inbox (64, 503 when full) and waits up to 60 s for the answer. Static files could be answered on the connection thread without reaching the frame, the way the 429 is. Whether they should is a design choice.
55	- `subscriber` (:878-927) uses `tungstenite::WebSocket::from_raw_socket` with no extensions negotiated.
56	- `local_address()` (:962-…) is the single IP the QR prints.
57	
58	### `src/app.rs` (routing and auth)
59	
60	- `serve_pending` (:1572-…) drains `port.poll(DRAIN_PER_PASS)` and calls `serve_remote` (:1595).
61	- `serve_remote` (:3017-3123):
62	  - `strip_prefix("/api/v1/")` with a 404 `not_found` for anything else (:3023-3025). This is the allowlist the issue means: `GET /` is refused here today.
63	  - `/info` and `/pair` are answered before `authenticate` (:3027-3031). `/events` is routed right after auth (:3036-3038).
64	  - The remainder is the §4.3 table, and the catch-all is 404 (:3109-3117).
65	- `authenticate` (:3127-3157) reads only `request.bearer`. Both 401 bodies use code `unauthorized`: "pair this device first" with no token, and "the token is not known; pair again" with an unknown token. **A revoked device and a device whose pairing was cleared by key rotation get the same answer.** Only the message differs from the no-token case.
66	- `remote_pair` (:3606-3674):
67	  - It requires the body's `spki_sha256` to equal the identity's and the code to match (upper-cased). Each mismatch dispatches `PairingFailed`.
68	  - `device_name` comes from the body (default "Device"). The host does not derive a name.
69	  - The reply is the enveloped `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}`. No header is set.
70	- `remote_info` (:3568-3604): `server_id`, `server_name`, `protocol`, `capabilities`, `spki_sha256`, `version`, `limits`, `pairing_open`.
71	- `remote_subscribe` (:2723-2759) needs `request.upgrade` and the subscriber queue, then sends `hello`. `scope=all` comes from the query.
72	- Revocation closes the device's sockets at :486-495 by dropping its subscriber queues. The connection thread then sends a WebSocket close with no code or reason (:893-899). The browser's next upgrade attempt is answered 401 (see Open questions on what the page can see of that).
73	- `refuse` (:3754-3772) logs `method` and `path` only. The query is never logged, so a `?code=` on `GET /` would not reach the log. **The code would still reach the frame inside `RemoteRequest.query`, sent by the browser in the request line before the page has run.**
74	- Bind (:2936-2990): loopback unless `identity.listen.lan`, which is the "Allow devices on the local network" checkbox (`src/ui/remote.rs:117-127`). §5 says "Require pairing **before** anything but `/info` and `/pair`". The issue's amendment adds the page's static files.
75	
76	### `src/ui/remote.rs` (dialog and QR)
77	
78	- `pairing` (:141-227) builds the QR payload as JSON `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}` (:160-166).
79	  - `addresses` is `local_address():port` **even when the port is bound to loopback only**, so a URL QR would point a phone at a closed port unless the dialog requires LAN first.
80	  - "Copy invite" copies the same JSON (:197-207). README :277 documents `switchboard-remote pair "$(pbpaste)"`.
81	- `qr_texture` (:279-299) encodes any string with `qrcode` 0.14, so a URL payload is a one-line change there.
82	- `devices` (:230-276) lists name, scope combo, paired, seen and Revoke. It shows no client kind.
83	- The redaction sentence is at :73-80. Decision 1's sentence on certificate trust would sit beside it.
84	
85	### `src/core/remote.rs`
86	
87	All pairing and device transitions are here (:21-103). Nothing in the core knows about HTTP. The scope is taken from the window (:166).
88	
89	### Native text path that must keep working
90	
91	- `client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:89-117`: `PairingInvite` is `Decodable` JSON. `parse(_:)` is a plain JSON decode, so it **does not accept a URL today**.
92	- `client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:107-127`: `pair '<json>'` or `pair <host:port> <code> <spki>`.
93	- The headset:

# Issue #230: a web control surface on the remote port (investigation notes)

I read CLAUDE.md, docs/lessons.md, docs/remote-client.md §§0, 4.1–4.7 and 5–6, and the remote section of docs/design.md (3107–3584). Line numbers below are as they stand in this worktree (branch `dispatch/230-…`, clean, at 7fe8949). There is no `web/` directory yet.

## The on-disk record and how it is rehydrated

Persistent state on the host is the same as today. The browser adds no new kind of record.

- **`<data dir>/devices.json`**, a `Vec<PairedDevice>` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96-106`): `id`, `name`, `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`. A browser is one more entry. The name is capped at 64 chars in `AppCore::new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs:159-170`), and the scope comes from the open window. It is written through `Effect::SaveDevices` (`src/app.rs:2910`). `last_seen` is saved at most every 300 s (`src/core/remote.rs:18`, `DeviceSeen` at 72-85). Nothing in the record says what kind of client a device is, so a "browser" field would be a schema change. The name string alone needs none.
- **`<data dir>/identity.json`** (`Identity`, `src/ports/remote.rs:26-41`, `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1` at :17): the server id, the name, the base64 DER certificate, `spki_sha256` and `listen {lan, port}`. The key sits in the Keychain under `remote-key:<server_id>`.
  - `make_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`) builds the certificate with `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`. So it has **no subjectAltName**, only a CN `Switchboard <id>`. Its validity is rcgen's default, which the doc comment gives as running to year 4096. It sets no EKU.
  - If the plan wants a certificate browsers accept more readily (SAN for the IP or a `.local` name, a shorter validity, serverAuth EKU, a download path), the certificate would have to be **reissued over the same key**. The SPKI and every native pin stay valid (§5 says so), but `identity.json`'s `certificate` changes. The file layout does not change.
  - A SAN tied to an IP would go stale when the address moves.
- **The pairing window** is core state only (`PairingWindow`: `until`, `code`, `scope`, `failures`; `src/core/remote.rs:45-52`) and is never saved. The QR payload is built in the UI from it every frame (`src/ui/remote.rs:154-172`).
- **The page itself** is compiled into the binary (`include_str!`), so there is nothing to rehydrate on the host. A page left open on a phone after the host updates itself keeps the old JS until it is reloaded. `/info` already carries `version` (`src/app.rs:3568-3604`).

Rehydration on the device lives in the browser, not in Switchboard:

- **The token** lives in a cookie jar or in `localStorage`, depending on decision 2.
- **The certificate exception** lives in the browser's store.
- **The flow on reload:**
  1. `GET /` with no auth.
  2. `GET /api/v1/info`.
  3. One authenticated read: 200 shows the sessions, 401 shows "pair again / revoked".
  4. Open `/api/v1/events`, then snapshot and reconcile per §4.4. A new `epoch` means refetch everything.

What the tree implies for rehydration:

- Host restart: same certificate, same tokens. The page reconnects and sees a new epoch.
- Key rotation (`src/app.rs:2776-2852` clears `devices.json`): the browser meets a **different certificate** at the same address. Its stored exception presumably no longer applies, so it shows its own interstitial before any page script runs. The page's "identity changed, pair again" state would then not be what the owner sees on a rotation. Whether that holds depends on how the browser scopes the exception (see Open questions).
- Address change (DHCP): a new origin. Cookies and `localStorage` are keyed by host, so the token is not found and the device pairs again, leaving the old record in `devices.json` until revoked.

## What exists, file by file

### `src/adapters/remote.rs` (listener, HTTP, WebSocket)

- `RemoteRequest` (:359-371) keeps only `method`, `path`, `query` (undecoded), `body`, `bearer` and `upgrade` (the `Sec-WebSocket-Key`).
  - `read_request` (:444-516) parses every header into a local `Vec` and then drops all but `content-length`, `authorization: Bearer`, `upgrade` and `sec-websocket-key`.
  - **No `Cookie`, `User-Agent`, `Origin`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, `Accept` or `If-None-Match` reaches the frame.** Decisions 2 and 6 and any Origin check need new fields here.
- `RemoteReply` (:389-393) is `{status, body, authenticated}`. **It carries no headers.**
  - `respond` (:530-553) writes `Content-Type: application/json` on every reply, plus `Content-Length` and `Connection: keep-alive`, and nothing else. It also has a fixed reason table.
  - Serving HTML/CSS/JS with their types, a CSP, `Cache-Control`, `Set-Cookie`, `X-Content-Type-Options` or a 304 needs `RemoteReply` (or a separate static path) to carry a content type and headers.
  - `respond_upgrade` (:519-527) writes a bare 101 with no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`.
  - These are adapter types, not `ports/` contract types, so changing them is not bound by the additive-only rule. Tests construct the request literal at :1045-1061.
- Pools and accept:
  - `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `MAX_PAIRED = 12` (:567-568).
  - The accept loop (:687-718) closes a 5th unauthenticated TCP connection **at accept, by dropping it**.
  - A connection moves to the paired pool only when a reply comes back with `authenticated: true` (:829-844).
  - So a browser fetching `/`, a CSS file, a JS file and `/api/v1/info` over parallel keep-alive connections stays wholly in the unauthenticated pool. That holds while the static replies are `authenticated: false`, and even with a cookie unless static replies authenticate.
  - Idle connections are held up to `IDLE_TIMEOUT = 30 s` (:573).
  - One browser can therefore fill the four slots and have its next connection dropped. That includes the one that would carry `/pair`.
- Rate windows: `Limits::limited` (:631-640) counts only `PAIR_PATH` (6/min) and `INFO_PATH` (60/min) (:583-587). A static path counts against nothing today. Note that **a page load that calls `/info` spends one of the 60**.
- Deadlines: 5 s for the handshake and the first request line (:570). A browser that opens a connection speculatively and sends nothing for 5 s is closed. That is harmless, but it holds a slot meanwhile.
- `connection` (:770-876) hands every request to the frame over the bounded inbox (64, 503 when full) and waits up to 60 s for the answer. Static files could be answered on the connection thread without reaching the frame, the way the 429 is. Whether they should is a design choice.
- `subscriber` (:878-927) uses `tungstenite::WebSocket::from_raw_socket` with no extensions negotiated.

- `authenticate` (:3127-3157) reads only `request.bearer`.   - It requires the body's `spki_sha256` to equal the identity's and the code to match (upper-cased). Each mismatch dispatches `PairingFailed`.
  - `device_name` comes from the body (default "Device"). The host does not derive a name.
  - The reply is the enveloped `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}`. No header is set.
- `remote_info` (:3568-3604): `server_id`, `server_name`, `protocol`, `capabilities`, `spki_sha256`, `version`, `limits`, `pairing_open`.
- `remote_subscribe` (:2723-2759) needs `request.upgrade` and the subscriber queue, then sends `hello`. `scope=all` comes from the query.
- Revocation closes the device's sockets at :486-495 by dropping its subscriber queues. The connection thread then sends a WebSocket close with no code or reason (:893-899). The browser's next upgrade attempt is answered 401 (see Open questions on what the page can see of that).

  - "Copy invite" copies the same JSON (:197-207). README :277 documents `switchboard-remote pair "$(pbpaste)"`.

- `devices` (:230-276) lists name, scope combo, paired, seen and Revoke. It shows no client kind.
- The redaction sentence is at :73-80. Decision 1's sentence on certificate trust would sit beside it.

All pairing and device transitions are here (:21-103). Nothing in the core knows about HTTP. The scope is taken from the window (:166).

10	- `make_identity` issues a certificate with no SAN, no EKU and a `not_after` in year 4096. Evidence: `src/adapters/remote.rs:90-110`.
11	- Apple's rules for TLS server certificates since iOS 13 and macOS 10.15 require the name in the SAN (the CN is ignored). Certificates issued after 2019-07-01 also need the serverAuth EKU and a validity of 825 days or less. Apple says connections that violate them "will fail". Evidence: https://support.apple.com/103769. Queries: "Apple requirements for trusted certificates iOS 13 macOS 10.15 self-signed certificate Safari subjectAltName 825 days".
12	- Secure context is decided by scheme: `https` and `wss` are "Potentially Trustworthy", and no certificate check takes part. So `crypto.randomUUID` is available to a page loaded after a click-through. Evidence: https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-secure-contexts/ §3.1 step 3. Queries: "secure context https certificate error click through isSecureContext Chrome Safari W3C secure contexts".
13	- WebSocket handshake: mode `websocket`, credentials mode `include`, so cookies go with it. Browsers MUST send `Origin` (RFC 6455 §4.1 item 8). Evidence: https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/, https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6455. Queries: "WHATWG WebSockets standard Sec-WebSocket-Protocol response must match requested protocol fail connection token"; "SameSite cookies WebSocket handshake cross-site WebSocket hijacking Chrome sends cookies Origin header".
14	- Subprotocol values are characters U+0021 to U+007E with no separators. Base64url without `=` padding fits; `=` does not. The constructor throws `SyntaxError` on an invalid value. If the client offered protocols and the 101 does not echo one, the browser fails the connection. Evidence: RFC 6455 §4.1 item 10 and §4.2.2; WHATWG WebSockets "establish a WebSocket connection" (same queries).
15	- A non-101 answer to an upgrade, such as a 401, reaches the page only as `error` followed by `close` with code 1006 and `wasClean` false. "User agents must not convey any failure information to scripts." The page cannot read the status from the socket; it must make a REST call to learn it. Evidence: https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ (same queries).
16	- Cookies are not isolated by port (RFC 6265 §8.5). A site is (scheme, host) with the port ignored, and an IP host has no registrable domain. So `https://<ip>:A` and `https://<ip>:B` are same-site, and a cookie set by one instance is sent to the other. Evidence: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#obtain-a-site, https://greenbytes.de/tech/specs/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-04.html. Queries: "RFC 6265 cookies do not provide isolation by port same IP address different port cookie shared".
17	- A URL fragment is never sent in the request line, and it is stripped from `Referer`. Evidence: https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-referrer-policy/ §8.4 step 5 ("Set url's fragment to null"); RFC 3986 §3.5. Queries: "URL fragment not sent to server HTTP request Referer fragment stripped RFC 9110 Fetch referrer policy".
18	- Chrome remembers a certificate-error bypass for 7 days, per host (the port is ignored and decisions are shared across schemes), keyed by error and certificate SHA-256. A new key is therefore a new certificate, which brings a fresh interstitial before any page script runs. Evidence: https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/HEAD/components/security_interstitials/content/stateful_ssl_host_state_delegate.cc (`kCertErrorBypassExpirationInSeconds = 604800`). Queries: "Chrome SSL certificate error "proceed" decision remembered how long per host chrome_ssl_host_state_delegate one week".

Evidence: https://searchfox.org/firefox-main/source/security/manager/ssl/nsICertOverrideService.idl. Query: "Firefox nsCertOverrideService override keyed host port fingerprint".
20	- Chrome's HTTP/1.1 pool allows 6 connections per host, and WebSockets have a separate cap of 255. Evidence: https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src.git/+/HEAD/net/socket/client_socket_pool_manager.cc. Queries: "Chrome maximum 6 connections per host HTTP/1.1 socket pool limit per group preconnect".

Evidence: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/technotes/tn3179-understanding-local-network-privacy (revision 2026-10-06). Queries: "iOS Local Network privacy permission Safari prompt connecting to private IP address web page TN3179".
22	- Chrome's Local Network Access prompt (Chrome 142) gates requests from public to local or loopback addresses. A private-IP page calling itself is not gated. Evidence: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/local-network-access (updated 2025-09-29). Queries: "Chrome Local Network Access permission prompt private IP page same origin requests exempt 2025".
23	- On iOS, a manually installed certificate profile is not trusted for TLS until the owner turns it on under Settings > General > About > Certificate Trust Settings. Evidence: https://support.apple.com/102390. Queries: "Apple support trust manually installed certificate profiles iOS Certificate Trust Settings enable full trust".
24

26	
27	- **Does Safari on iOS offer a click-through for the current certificate (no SAN, no EKU, validity to 4096)? Does Chrome, whose error is `COMMON_NAME_INVALID`?** Tried: the Apple and Chrome queries above. Apple says only that non-compliant connections "fail". Practitioner posts (https://bugzilla.cendio.com/show_bug.cgi?id=7401) report that a SAN fixed iOS 13. No vendor page says whether the interstitial stays bypassable. If favourable, the plan may keep the certificate as issued. If unfavourable, and as the line to build to either way: reissue the certificate over the same key with a SAN (the LAN IP and `<host>.local`), the serverAuth EKU and a validity of 825 days or less, with renewal before expiry. 1	# Issue #230: a web control surface on the remote port (investigation notes)
2	
3	I read CLAUDE.md, docs/lessons.md, docs/remote-client.md §§0, 4.1–4.7 and 5–6, and the remote section of docs/design.md (3107–3584). Line numbers below are as they stand in this worktree (branch `dispatch/230-…`, clean, at 7fe8949). There is no `web/` directory yet.
4	
5	## The on-disk record and how it is rehydrated
6	
7	Persistent state on the host is the same as today. The browser adds no new kind of record.
8	
9	- **`<data dir>/devices.json`**, a `Vec<PairedDevice>` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96-106`): `id`, `name`, `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`. A browser is one more entry. The name is capped at 64 chars in `AppCore::new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs:159-170`), and the scope comes from the open window. It is written through `Effect::SaveDevices` (`src/app.rs:2910`). `last_seen` is saved at most every 300 s (`src/core/remote.rs:18`, `DeviceSeen` at 72-85). Nothing in the record says what kind of client a device is, so a "browser" field would be a schema change. The name string alone needs none.
10	- **`<data dir>/identity.json`** (`Identity`, `src/ports/remote.rs:26-41`, `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1` at :17): the server id, the name, the base64 DER certificate, `spki_sha256` and `listen {lan, port}`. The key sits in the Keychain under `remote-key:<server_id>`.
11	  - `make_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`) builds the certificate with `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`. So it has **no subjectAltName**, only a CN `Switchboard <id>`. Its validity is rcgen's default, which the doc comment gives as running to year 4096. It sets no EKU.
12	  - If the plan wants a certificate browsers accept more readily (SAN for the IP or a `.local` name, a shorter validity, serverAuth EKU, a download path), the certificate would have to be **reissued over the same key**. The SPKI and every native pin stay valid (§5 says so), but `identity.json`'s `certificate` changes. The file layout does not change.
13	  - A SAN tied to an IP would go stale when the address moves.
14	- **The pairing window** is core state only (`PairingWindow`: `until`, `code`, `scope`, `failures`; `src/core/remote.rs:45-52`) and is never saved. The QR payload is built in the UI from it every frame (`src/ui/remote.rs:154-172`).
15	- **The page itself** is compiled into the binary (`include_str!`), so there is nothing to rehydrate on the host. A page left open on a phone after the host updates itself keeps the old JS until it is reloaded. `/info` already carries `version` (`src/app.rs:3568-3604`).
16	
17	Rehydration on the device lives in the browser, not in Switchboard:
18	
19	- **The token** lives in a cookie jar or in `localStorage`, depending on decision 2.
20	- **The certificate exception** lives in the browser's store.
21	- **The flow on reload:**
22	  1. `GET /` with no auth.
23	  2. `GET /api/v1/info`.
24	  3. One authenticated read: 200 shows the sessions, 401 shows "pair again / revoked".
25	  4. Open `/api/v1/events`, then snapshot and reconcile per §4.4. A new `epoch` means refetch everything.
26	
27	What the tree implies for rehydration:
28	
29	- Host restart: same certificate, same tokens. The page reconnects and sees a new epoch.
30	- Key rotation (`src/app.rs:2776-2852` clears `devices.json`): the browser meets a **different certificate** at the same address. Its stored exception presumably no longer applies, so it shows its own interstitial before any page script runs. The page's "identity changed, pair again" state would then not be what the owner sees on a rotation. Whether that holds depends on how the browser scopes the exception (see Open questions).
31	- Address change (DHCP): a new origin. Cookies and `localStorage` are keyed by host, so the token is not found and the device pairs again, leaving the old record in `devices.json` until revoked.

33	## What exists, file by file
34	
35	### `src/adapters/remote.rs` (listener, HTTP, WebSocket)
36	
37	- `RemoteRequest` (:359-371) keeps only `method`, `path`, `query` (undecoded), `body`, `bearer` and `upgrade` (the `Sec-WebSocket-Key`).
38	  - `read_request` (:444-516) parses every header into a local `Vec` and then drops all but `content-length`, `authorization: Bearer`, `upgrade` and `sec-websocket-key`.
39	  - **No `Cookie`, `User-Agent`, `Origin`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, `Accept` or `If-None-Match` reaches the frame.** Decisions 2 and 6 and any Origin check need new fields here.
40	- `RemoteReply` (:389-393) is `{status, body, authenticated}`. **It carries no headers.**
41	  - `respond` (:530-553) writes `Content-Type: application/json` on every reply, plus `Content-Length` and `Connection: keep-alive`, and nothing else. It also has a fixed reason table.
42	  - Serving HTML/CSS/JS with their types, a CSP, `Cache-Control`, `Set-Cookie`, `X-Content-Type-Options` or a 304 needs `RemoteReply` (or a separate static path) to carry a content type and headers.
43	  - `respond_upgrade` (:519-527) writes a bare 101 with no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`.
44	  - These are adapter types, not `ports/` contract types, so changing them is not bound by the additive-only rule. Tests construct the request literal at :1045-1061.
45	- Pools and accept:
46	  - `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `MAX_PAIRED = 12` (:567-568).
47	  - The accept loop (:687-718) closes a 5th unauthenticated TCP connection **at accept, by dropping it**.
48	  - A connection moves to the paired pool only when a reply comes back with `authenticated: true` (:829-844).
49	  - So a browser fetching `/`, a CSS file, a JS file and `/api/v1/info` over parallel keep-alive connections stays wholly in the unauthenticated pool. That holds while the static replies are `authenticated: false`, and even with a cookie unless static replies authenticate.
50	  - Idle connections are held up to `IDLE_TIMEOUT = 30 s` (:573).
51	  - One browser can therefore fill the four slots and have its next connection dropped. That includes the one that would carry `/pair`.
52	- Rate windows: `Limits::limited` (:631-640) counts only `PAIR_PATH` (6/min) and `INFO_PATH` (60/min) (:583-587). A static path counts against nothing today. Note that **a page load that calls `/info` spends one of the 60**.
53	- Deadlines: 5 s for the handshake and the first request line (:570). A browser that opens a connection speculatively and sends nothing for 5 s is closed. That is harmless, but it holds a slot meanwhile.
54	- `connection` (:770-876) hands every request to the frame over the bounded inbox (64, 503 when full) and waits up to 60 s for the answer. Static files could be answered on the connection thread without reaching the frame, the way the 429 is. Whether they should is a design choice.
55	- `subscriber` (:878-927) uses `tungstenite::WebSocket::from_raw_socket` with no extensions negotiated.
56	- `local_address()` (:962-…) is the single IP the QR prints.

59	
60	- `serve_pending` (:1572-…) drains `port.poll(DRAIN_PER_PASS)` and calls `serve_remote` (:1595).
61	- `serve_remote` (:3017-3123):
62	  - `strip_prefix("/api/v1/")` with a 404 `not_found` for anything else (:3023-3025). This is the allowlist the issue means: `GET /` is refused here today.
63	  - `/info` and `/pair` are answered before `authenticate` (:3027-3031). `/events` is routed right after auth (:3036-3038).

65	- `authenticate` (:3127-3157) reads only `request.bearer`. Both 401 bodies use code `unauthorized`: "pair this device first" with no token, and "the token is not known; pair again" with an unknown token. **A revoked device and a device whose pairing was cleared by key rotation get the same answer.** Only the message differs from the no-token case.
66	- `remote_pair` (:3606-3674):
67	  - It requires the body's `spki_sha256` to equal the identity's and the code to match (upper-cased). Each mismatch dispatches `PairingFailed`.

73	- `refuse` (:3754-3772) logs `method` and `path` only. The query is never logged, so a `?code=` on `GET /` would not reach the log. **The code would still reach the frame inside `RemoteRequest.query`, sent by the browser in the request line before the page has run.**

121	## Things a plan has to account for that the tree already decides
122	
123	- The first navigation `GET /?code=…&key=…&id=…` puts the code in the **request line**, so whoever terminates TLS at that address sees it before the page's script compares keys. The URL also carries `key`, so a terminator that received both could post `/pair` to the real host with the right key.
124	  - Under click-through trust, an active impostor serves its own script anyway, as the issue says. So the key-in-URL check defends only against an honest wrong host, for example a second Switchboard instance on another port or a stale address.
125	  - Whether the parameters ride in the query or the fragment is the planner's choice. The difference between the two in what the server receives is listed as a [source] question.
126	- Two instances on one Mac (supported; the test at :1464) share an IP. Cookies are per host and not per port, and a second instance has its own token for a different `server_id`. A cookie name not keyed by `server_id` would collide between them. `localStorage` is per origin (port included).
127	- `/pair` takes the device name from the body. The host would derive a name from the User-Agent only if `read_request` keeps that header.
128	- The pre-pairing surface (`/info` and `/pair` plus static files) and the rate windows live in `Limits` and `serve_remote`. The 4-slot unauthenticated pool is shared by everything a browser does before it authenticates.
129	- `SWITCHBOARD_SCRIPT` already has `pairing <code>|close`, `remote-devices` and `remote-listen lan|loopback <port>` (README :318-319), so the live acceptance can be staged without clicking.

1	# Facts for issue #230 (web control surface)
2	
3	No spike was run. No Chrome or Firefox is installed here, and Safari's certificate interstitial needs a person's tap. Sources were read on 2026-10-22.
4	
5	## Settled
6	
7	- No reply tells a paired device its current scope except the `/pair` reply. `/info` has none. A raise or drop is only seen as a 403 `scope` on a command. Evidence: `src/app.rs:3568-3604`, `:3662`, `:3166-3171`.
8	- Two things parse the QR text: `PairingInvite.parse`, from `switchboard-remote pair` (`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:111`), and the headset's paste and `SWITCHBOARD_INVITE` (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:106`, `:883`). The README documents `pbpaste` (`README.md:277`). Dispatch does not read it.
9	- `local_address()` takes the source address of the default route to `192.0.2.1`. With a full-tunnel VPN up, that is the VPN interface's address. The QR prints it even while the port is bound to loopback. Evidence: `src/adapters/remote.rs:962-970`, `src/ui/remote.rs:155-166`.
10	- `make_identity` issues a certificate with no SAN, no EKU and a `not_after` in year 4096. Evidence: `src/adapters/remote.rs:90-110`.
11	- Apple's rules for TLS server certificates since iOS 13 and macOS 10.15 require the name in the SAN (the CN is ignored). Certificates issued after 2019-07-01 also need the serverAuth EKU and a validity of 825 days or less. Apple says connections that violate them "will fail". Evidence: https://support.apple.com/103769. Queries: "Apple requirements for trusted certificates iOS 13 macOS 10.15 self-signed certificate Safari subjectAltName 825 days".
12	- Secure context is decided by scheme: `https` and `wss` are "Potentially Trustworthy", and no certificate check takes part. So `crypto.randomUUID` is available to a page loaded after a click-through. Evidence: https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-secure-contexts/ §3.1 step 3. Queries: "secure context https certificate error click through isSecureContext Chrome Safari W3C secure contexts".
13	- WebSocket handshake: mode `websocket`, credentials mode `include`, so cookies go with it. Browsers MUST send `Origin` (RFC 6455 §4.1 item 8). Evidence: https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/, https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6455. Queries: "WHATWG WebSockets standard Sec-WebSocket-Protocol response must match requested protocol fail connection token"; "SameSite cookies WebSocket handshake cross-site WebSocket hijacking Chrome sends cookies Origin header".
14	- Subprotocol values are characters U+0021 to U+007E with no separators. Base64url without `=` padding fits; `=` does not. The constructor throws `SyntaxError` on an invalid value. If the client offered protocols and the 101 does not echo one, the browser fails the connection. Evidence: RFC 6455 §4.1 item 10 and §4.2.2; WHATWG WebSockets "establish a WebSocket connection" (same queries).
15	- A non-101 answer to an upgrade, such as a 401, reaches the page only as `error` followed by `close` with code 1006 and `wasClean` false. "User agents must not convey any failure information to scripts." The page cannot read the status from the socket; it must make a REST call to learn it. Evidence: https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ (same queries).
16	- Cookies are not isolated by port (RFC 6265 §8.5). A site is (scheme, host) with the port ignored, and an IP host has no registrable domain. So `https://<ip>:A` and `https://<ip>:B` are same-site, and a cookie set by one instance is sent to the other. Evidence: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#obtain-a-site, https://greenbytes.de/tech/specs/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-04.html. Queries: "RFC 6265 cookies do not provide isolation by port same IP address different port cookie shared".
17	- A URL fragment is never sent in the request line, and it is stripped from `Referer`. Evidence: https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-referrer-policy/ §8.4 step 5 ("Set url's fragment to null"); RFC 3986 §3.5. Queries: "URL fragment not sent to server HTTP request Referer fragment stripped RFC 9110 Fetch referrer policy".
18	- Chrome remembers a certificate-error bypass for 7 days, per host (the port is ignored and decisions are shared across schemes), keyed by error and certificate SHA-256. A new key is therefore a new certificate, which brings a fresh interstitial before any page script runs. Evidence: https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/HEAD/components/security_interstitials/content/stateful_ssl_host_state_delegate.cc (`kCertErrorBypassExpirationInSeconds = 604800`). Queries: "Chrome SSL certificate error "proceed" decision remembered how long per host chrome_ssl_host_state_delegate one week".
19	- Firefox keys an override by host:port, certificate fingerprint and origin attributes, so a rotated key brings a new interstitial. Evidence: https://searchfox.org/firefox-main/source/security/manager/ssl/nsICertOverrideService.idl. Query: "Firefox nsCertOverrideService override keyed host port fingerprint".
20	- Chrome's HTTP/1.1 pool allows 6 connections per host, and WebSockets have a separate cap of 255. Evidence: https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src.git/+/HEAD/net/socket/client_socket_pool_manager.cc. Queries: "Chrome maximum 6 connections per host HTTP/1.1 socket pool limit per group preconnect".
21	- Safari, `SFSafariViewController` and `WKWebView` traffic does not need iOS Local Network permission, so there is no prompt. Evidence: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/technotes/tn3179-understanding-local-network-privacy (revision 2026-10-06). Queries: "iOS Local Network privacy permission Safari prompt connecting to private IP address web page TN3179".
22	- Chrome's Local Network Access prompt (Chrome 142) gates requests from public to local or loopback addresses. A private-IP page calling itself is not gated. Evidence: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/local-network-access (updated 2025-09-29). Queries: "Chrome Local Network Access permission prompt private IP page same origin requests exempt 2025".
23	- On iOS, a manually installed certificate profile is not trusted for TLS until the owner turns it on under Settings > General > About > Certificate Trust Settings. Evidence: https://support.apple.com/102390. Queries: "Apple support trust manually installed certificate profiles iOS Certificate Trust Settings enable full trust".
